story.title: A sentence can be fluent and still be the wrong translation
paragraphs: Surrounding sentences can decide whom a pronoun refers to, or whether “They returned to the bank” means a riverbank or a financial institution. WMT human annotators have rated translations with document context since 2019, yet most metrics still score one sentence at a time, without the evidence the annotators had.

Adding context only at inference is not enough: a metric trained on single sentences has not learned to separate a good surrounding passage from a bad target sentence, so a prepended paragraph shifts its input and can blur the judgment. Cont-COMET selects relevant context and trains with it.

mechanism.title: Context changes the representation; the target still determines the score
paragraphs: Cont-COMET extends COMET-21, the 2021 release of the COMET neural metric. Source, hypothesis, and reference are each encoded with surrounding sentences, but pooling covers only the current sentence's tokens, so the score still describes the target. The hypothesis is surrounded by reference context, not by neighboring machine translations that carry their own errors; using the hypothesis's own context lowers system-level correlation (Table 3).

Fine-tuning uses WMT20 Direct Assessment (DA) ratings matched to their documents, because WMT19 lacks document metadata and WMT21–22 DA scores were not available. Expert MQM (Multidimensional Quality Metrics) judgments from WMT21 and WMT22, averaged over en-de, en-ru, and zh-en, are the test sets.

evidence.title: Context-aware training, not context alone, protects sentence-level scores
paragraphs: The informative comparison is with COMET-21 given the same six context sentences without retraining. On WMT22 that inference-only variant ranks systems best but has the lowest segment-level correlation, while the trained metric gives up a little system-level correlation for the highest segment τ (Table 2). On WMT21 News, inference-only context lowers both levels; Cont-COMET restores system correlation, but its segment τ stays slightly below COMET-21's.

In Table 3, removing selection changes WMT22 correlations only from 0.943 to 0.942 (system) and from 0.354 to 0.353 (segment). Training without context but testing with it reproduces the inference-only pattern, and training with preceding sentences alone is worse on every reported measure. Training under the conditions of use carries the gain; selection is a small refinement.

reading_notes: Re-read full method and result/ablation tables. Distinguish system Pearson from segment Kendall. Demo reproduces the selection formula on authored text and hand-set similarities; it does not run COMET or score translations.

demo.title: Which context reaches the evaluator?
demo.description: Cont-COMET scores every reference sentence in the document by cosine similarity to the current sentence, discounted by α for each sentence of distance, keeps the highest-scoring ones up to a budget, and restores document order (Section 2.2). Here the current reference contains the ambiguous word “bank” (river bank or financial bank). Change the budget, the decay factor, the eligible side, and the similarities.
demo.note: Illustrative: the document, its cosine similarities and every α value (the paper does not report α); the default similarities make the nearest previous sentence uninformative, so that selection and an adjacent window disagree. Adapted: the selection rule from Section 2.2. Computed: selection scores and the chosen context. As α falls, selection approaches an adjacent window of the same size; as α approaches 1, distant but similar sentences compete. No model or translation metric runs here.
